title: Bayesian Test-Time Adaptation for Motor Imagery EEG Decoding
one_liner: When an EEG decoder meets a new person or new brain state, instead of retraining it with gradient descent, map the brain's noisy signal into a compact space of known healthy patterns, then fuse that record with the model's prior guess to fix the answer.
lead: An EEG-based brain-computer interface (BCI) decodes motor imagery: the user thinks move your hand and the system reads that intent from brain waves to control a cursor or limb. The problem is that EEG signals are catastrophically noisy, and every new person and every new session produces different signal patterns. Retraining the model for each new person is expensive and fragile. This paper proposes BTTA-DG: a new way to adapt the decoder on-the-fly during real-time inference (when the user is actually using it), by treating the messy new signals as samples from a known family of patterns and fusing them with the model's initial guess to make honest predictions.

problem.h2: Brain signals are never the same twice
paras: An EEG motor-imagery BCI reads 64 electrodes pasted on your scalp to detect whether you are imagining left-hand movement or right-hand movement. In the lab, the model trains on 100 imagined movements from person A, learns a mapping from electrode patterns to intent, and achieves 90% accuracy. But on day 2, the same person A sits down, the electrodes sit slightly differently, their coffee intake changed their vigilance, their posture shifted, and suddenly the model drops to 60% accuracy. Moreover, person B sits down and the model bottoms out at 20%. The raw brain signals look radically different from one session to the next.

The naive fix is gradient descent: take the new person's unlabeled data (just the brain waves, no labels), compute gradients that would make the model confident on those new signals, and nudge the weights. But this breaks in two ways. First, it is expensive and slow—a BCI needs real-time response, not a minute of computation. Second, if you are not careful with the learning rate, the model forgets the old task entirely and becomes useless. Other methods try to align where the signals cluster in the new person to match where they clustered in the old person, but they miss the deeper problem: the temporal structure of the new signal has shifted, not just the overall shape. A person's brain state drifts over time within a single session.

callout.html: Instead of retraining, map each raw noisy signal into a learned compact space where healthy patterns cluster, then treat the stream of mapped signals as evidence of the person's current brain state, and fuse that evidence with the model's initial confidence to produce honest, calibrated predictions.

steps.text: A large cross-subject EEG dataset trains a shared feature encoder.
Map temporal embeddings into a Dirichlet space (learned low-dimensional simplex) where healthy patterns cluster in predictable ways.
On historical data, fit a Gaussian Mixture Model (a family of blurred bells) of the Dirichlet space to capture normal variation.
Real-time: each raw signal block is extracted, projected, and lands as a point in the Dirichlet space.
The accumulated Dirichlet samples update belief over the person's brain state; Bayesian inference fuses this with the model's prior, yielding calibrated class predictions.

object.h2: What the method changes: the output calibration
paras: The method does not retrain the classifier weights at all. Instead, it changes what happens after the model's raw prediction. Normally, the model outputs a confidence score (like 0.7 for left-hand, 0.3 for right-hand). The paper's trick is to treat those raw scores as one piece of evidence and fuse them with a separate estimate of what brain state this person is in right now, based on the stream of signals accumulated so far. This fusion happens at inference time, zero gradient updates, zero new learnable weights. Only the output confidence scores change.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: concentration of brain state
hidden.name: Dirichlet concentration—how sharply focused the person's brain state is
paras: Imagine a person's brain state is not fixed: it wanders slightly over time due to fatigue, focus level (how sharp or dull your mental state is), or posture. The paper's hidden quantity measures how tightly the person is clustered in their current state—are they right on top of one canonical brain pattern, or are they spread across many? In math, this is captured by the parameters of a Dirichlet distribution (a way to model fuzzy memberships, like how much your effort is split across three tasks). High concentration means the person's signals consistently project to a tight region. Low concentration means they are all over the place.

The paper estimates this concentration by fitting a Gaussian Mixture Model to the historical Dirichlet projections. That model acts as a 'map of normal brain states.' When new signals arrive, each one is projected to the Dirichlet space and compared to that map. If the new sample lands in a high-probability region of the map, concentration is high and the Bayesian inference is confident. If the new sample lands in a weird region, concentration is low and the inference backs off to the prior.

heat.caption: Darker cells mean higher concentration (person's signals cluster tightly in Dirichlet space).

reads.html: The concentration is how tight or spread-out the new person's brain signals are when plotted in the learned projection space. Tight clusters mean confident adaptation; spread-out points mean uncertain, so back off.

The paper models the Dirichlet parameters with a Gaussian Mixture Model fitted to cross-subject training data, then evaluates the likelihood of new samples under that GMM to infer concentration and trust.

mechanism.h2: Why Bayesian fusion works better than retraining
paras: Here is the causal chain. The pretrained model has never seen the new person, so its raw predictions are miscalibrated—overconfident or underconfident compared to reality. Gradient-based retraining tries to fix this by moving weights, but weights are shared across all people and all classes, so one person's update corrupts the model for everyone else. Instead, the paper decouples: the weights stay frozen, and only the output probabilities are adjusted. This adjustment happens via Bayesian inference, which is principled and reversible. The mechanism: (1) Project the new person's signals into a compact Dirichlet space where the trained encoder already knows how to place them. (2) Fit a Gaussian Mixture Model to that space on historical data, so we have a map of normal patterns. (3) When new signals arrive, evaluate how likely they are under that map (likelihood score). (4) Fuse the likelihood with the model's initial guess: new confidence is proportional to (initial guess) times (likelihood) divided by normalizer. If the new signals are in a high-likelihood region, the model's guess gets reinforced. If they are in a low-likelihood region (weird for this person), the model's guess is pulled back toward uniform. This is mathematically conservative—it never invents confidence where none is justified. It also runs in near-real-time because the Dirichlet projection is a single forward pass (no backprop), and the Bayesian fusion is a lookup in the GMM and one multiplication.

Why does this fix the two problems? First, no catastrophic forgetting—weights never change, so the old task is always preserved. Second, it captures temporal structure—each raw Dirichlet sample is independent, but the stream of samples tells a story about how this person's brain state is evolving within the session. The GMM learned from cross-subject data generalizes that temporal structure to a new person automatically.

stages.s: Fuse with model prior via Bayes rule

math.words: Posterior class probability equals prior times likelihood, divided by the evidence.
math.equation: P(class | new_signal) = P(new_signal | concentration) * P(class | pretrained) / P(new_signal)
symbols: Posterior: the updated confidence in the class after seeing this new signal.
Likelihood: how probable this signal is, given the person's current brain state (from GMM).
Prior: the model's baseline confidence before adaptation.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Say the pretrained model, seeing a new person, predicts 60% left-hand, 40% right-hand (the prior).

A raw signal arrives and projects into the Dirichlet space. The trained GMM says this signal is 90% likely for a left-handed person (likelihood = 0.9 for left, 0.5 for right, lower because right rarely produces this pattern).
The model's 60% left guess got pushed up to 73%, because the new signal looks like a left-pattern. Over many signals, this accumulates and converges to the true intent.

math.note: Bayes rule ensures that even if the model's prior is bad, the likelihood from the Dirichlet patterns pulls the prediction toward truth without retraining.

charts.title: Naive gradient-based fine-tuning
charts.note: Retraining fixes the new person but catastrophically forgets the old task.

charts.title: This paper (Bayesian adaptation)
charts.note: No forgetting—old task remains perfect, new person improved, and inference is real-time.

items.b: The GMM is fitted to cross-subject data and misses individual outliers.
items.html: If a new person's brain state is genuinely rare (e.g., a neurological disorder), the trained GMM will assign low likelihood to their signals, and the Bayesian fusion will remain anchored to the prior instead of adapting. The method is only as good as the diversity of the training cohort.

items.b: Dirichlet projection is lossy and may discard signal structure.
items.html: Mapping high-dimensional temporal embeddings to a low-dimensional Dirichlet space saves computation, because you are squeezing many numbers into few numbers, which is fast. But this squeeze risks throwing away subtle patterns, because when you compress information into fewer numbers, some of the original detail gets lost—like photographing a face in low resolution. If the original signal contains high-frequency artifacts or rare motor patterns, the projection may smooth them away and miss them.

items.b: Streaming adaptation has a lag: the first few signals are adapted with almost no evidence.
items.html: In the first 0.5 seconds of a new session, only a handful of signal blocks have arrived. The GMM's likelihood estimate is noisy, and the Bayesian fusion is weak. Accuracy at t=0 to t=1s is still near the prior, not the true adapted confidence.

The paper validates on held-out subjects and sessions, showing that the method generalizes to new people despite the limitations. Real-time speed is confirmed, and comparisons to other EEG-TTA methods are thorough.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small EEG motor-imagery dataset (4 subjects, 20 left and 20 right imaginations per subject per session, 64 electrodes, sampled at 250 Hz). Pretrain an encoder (a network that extracts signal patterns) on three subjects' data. On the held-out fourth subject, measure accuracy in two settings: (a) zero-shot (model runs on the new subject with no adaptation, purely prior predictions), and (b) with Bayesian adaptation (model fuses new subject's live signals with the Dirichlet GMM, adapting the output probabilities). Track accuracy over time as more signals accumulate. Also measure forgetting by checking whether the adapted model still predicts correctly on the held-out third subject's test set (it should, because weights never changed).
demo.metric_eq: Accuracy gain from adaptation = (accuracy after 50 signals) - (zero-shot accuracy before any signal). Forgetting = (pre-adaptation accuracy on old subject) - (post-adaptation accuracy on old subject), should be near zero.
demo.closing: The demo must show that without weight retraining, Bayesian adaptation can narrow the gap between a model trained on one person and a new person in real-time.
